author: Majid Maleki Meighani
title: The Radicalism of Form and the Radicalism of Content
content:
The wave of high-school protests in France, which began in late September 2026 in the suburbs of Paris and spread to many other cities, has revived an old question on the radical left: is a riot left-wing simply because its form is radical? Drawing on the Marxist tradition, this article separates three levels of analysis: the social cause of a protest, the form the struggle takes, and its political direction. It argues that these do not necessarily coincide. The legitimacy of a demand does not guarantee the legitimacy of every form of action. The radicalism of a form of struggle does not guarantee the radicalism of its political content. And the political outcome of a movement is not necessarily what its first participants intended. The left’s criterion should be neither the intensity of images from the street nor even the form of action itself, but the capacity to convert scattered anger into organized social power. The article warns against two traps at once: glorifying disorder for its own sake, and accepting the frame in which the state reduces every protest to “urban violence.”

The current protests in France began with entirely material grievances: a shortage of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, decaying school buildings, mounting pressure to perform, and anxiety about a future that looks less secure to much of this generation than it did to the last. author: Tahrir Hamdi
title: Palestine Resists: From Fanon and Kanafani to Armed Struggle and Return
content:
How does one resist dispossession and displacement, ongoing genocide, culturicide, scholasticide and epistemicide, and all forms of erasure of a people’s past, present and future? The answer: Resist by all available means—armed resistance, cultural resistance, and economic resistance; this is a legal right recognized under international law, but before that, it is morally legitimate, justified, and necessary. Israel is a brutal settler colony that was made possible by two main strategies: the expulsion of the Palestinian people from their indigenous land (historic Palestine) and ongoing genocide that is now 78 years old.

Armed resistance, as theorized by anti-colonial theorists such as Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Amílcar Cabral, Ghassan Kanafani, and Edward Said, is an essential part of the anti-colonial struggle for the liberation of colonized minds and lands. In his book The Wretched of the Earth (1963), Frantz Fanon, a psychiatrist by training, forcefully argued for anti-colonial armed resistance, stating precisely because colonization is such a violent and dehumanizing process, “decolonization is always a violent phenomenon” (35). author: Binoy Kampmark
title: Sportswashing the Racing Circuit: Rwanda and Formula One
content:
Tyrants and demagogues love sports and the governing bodies that preside over them. Despite strictures, injunctions and warnings about dealing with unsavoury regimes, a sporting body or organisation can always be relied on to ignore the fine print of their charters and make a dash for the revenue till. While the candidates for such a list are long – the International Olympic Committee and the world footballing body FIFA figure with amoral sprightliness in that regard – Formula One (F1) has shown itself to be most promiscuous.

In its October 13 statement, FI glows with the announcement that motor racing will “return to Africa for the first time since 1993.” Then, the apartheid government of South Africa, one nearing expiration, still offered their good services to F1 to run the tournament as part of a controversial tradition. (The South African Grand Prix had been something of a fixture since the 1960s, barring the interrupting hiccup in the latter 1980s.) In a ten-year agreement with the Rwandan government, the Formula 1 African Grand Prix will become a part of the racing calendar in the early 2030s, beginning its first race at the still to be completed Bugesera circuit. “The new track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards as part of a wider sports, tourism, infrastructure, and commercial development project led by the Rwanda Development Board.”

author: Ramzy Baroud
title: What Does the Green Party’s Historic Anti-Zionist Motion Mean for Palestine?
content:
The Green Party has put the conversation back on track: the problem is not the lack of creative solutions to the Israeli occupation of Palestine. The problem is Zionism itself.

To appreciate the significance of Motion A105, adopted by the Green Party of England and Wales on October 4, consider its basic tenets.

The party is now formally anti-Zionist. It endorses the Palestinian right of return, supports one democratic state throughout historic Palestine, reaffirms its commitment to the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS) movement, distinguishes anti-Zionism from antisemitism, and calls for a full arms embargo against Israel.

Though the decision may seem revolutionary within British politics, it is hardly revolutionary when examined against the history of Palestinian dispossession, beginning long before the Nakba of 1948.

Indeed, the Greens were not the first to equate Zionism with racism. That history owes much to Africa’s anti-colonial movements and their struggle against apartheid.

In 1975, the Organization of African Unity, meeting in Kampala, Uganda, drew explicit parallels between the racial systems governing South Africa, Rhodesia and occupied Palestine, identifying their common imperialist origins.
